title: Money and Wise Choices
objectives: I can explain what ten words about money and choices mean.
I can use words like income, expense, and profit to tell how money comes in and goes out.
I can use the endings -y and -able to understand words like thrifty and affordable.
I can write about a money choice and give reasons.
rationale: Money words connect math word problems, social studies, and real life, and they let students weigh consequences in a practical setting. The ten words fall into three groups: how money moves (income, expense, profit, debt, budget), how people buy (afford, purchase, bargain), and how they act (thrifty, wealthy). Students use them to follow a character who plans, earns, and spends. The story repeats the cause-and-effect language of unit 2 (because of, as a result) in a real situation and builds on sensible choices and gadgets from earlier units.

passage.title: Zoe's Lemonade Plan
paras: Zoe wanted a new bicycle, but it cost sixty dollars, and she could not afford it with her small allowance. Her grandmother, who was thrifty, said, "Make a budget, and you will see how to reach your goal."

Zoe made a list. Her only income was her allowance, so she decided to sell lemonade on Saturdays. She wrote down each expense: lemons, sugar, cups, and a poster. At the grocery store, she found a bargain on sugar and saved three dollars. Her brother lent her five dollars for the cups, which put her in debt for a week. She wrote "Pay Luis back" at the bottom of her list.

After three Saturdays, Zoe counted her money. She had earned fifty-five dollars. Her expenses were ten dollars, so her profit was forty-five dollars. She paid her brother back at once. "I am not wealthy," she laughed, "but I am getting closer."
With her profit and fifteen dollars of allowance, Zoe went to the shop and made her purchase: a bright blue bicycle. "A plan is the best tool I have," she said. Her grandmother smiled.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, what does the word "bargain" mean?
choices: Something that costs less than it is worth
qs.why: Zoe found sugar for less money and saved three dollars, so it was a good deal.

choices: The money left after expenses are paid
qs.why: Zoe's earnings minus her expenses leave her profit of forty-five dollars.

qs.q: Why did Zoe's grandmother tell her to make a budget?
choices: She wanted Zoe to stop buying anything
A plan would show Zoe how to reach her goal
She planned to buy the bicycle herself
She thought Zoe should spend her allowance right away
qs.why: Her grandmother said the budget would show how to reach the goal of buying the bicycle.

qs.q: Which detail shows Zoe was in debt for a short time?
choices: Her brother lent her five dollars for cups, and she wrote that she needed to pay him back.
qs.why: Borrowing five dollars and writing a reminder to repay shows the debt.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Lemonade is the best business for kids.
Bicycles are cheaper than they used to be.
A plan for earning and spending money can help you reach a goal.
qs.why: Zoe makes a budget, earns money, and buys the bicycle.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten money words through the story of a girl who makes a plan to buy a bicycle. They sort the words into how money moves, how people buy, and how people act, and they use them in word problems and short writing.

notes.va.budget.n: Show a simple two-column budget with income and expenses. Be sensitive that some families have little money; use fictional examples instead of asking about home finances.
notes.va.afford.v: Afford is about whether the money is enough. Practice with a menu and play money. Avoid asking students what their families can or cannot afford.
notes.va.bargain.n: Bargain has two senses: a good price and an agreement. The first is the main sense. Ask which sense a sentence uses.
notes.va.profit.n: Profit is what is left after costs. Use a lemonade stand with simple numbers. Students often think profit is all the money taken in.
notes.va.expense.n: An expense is money going out. Pair with income: one comes in, one goes out. Use arrows on the board.
notes.va.thrifty.adj: Thrifty is positive: careful with money. Distinguish from stingy, which is unkind. Thrift + -y.
notes.va.wealthy.adj: Wealth + -y. Avoid judging people by wealth; talk about how money can be used. Contrast with the word poor only with care.
notes.va.purchase.v: More formal than buy; use it in writing about receipts and orders. The noun purchase means the thing you bought.
notes.va.debt.n: The b is silent. Debt is money owed. Use a fictional example, such as borrowing from a friend, and show the steps to pay it off.
notes.va.income.n: In + come: money that comes in. Pair with expense. Students often confuse income with profit: income is all that comes in; profit is what is left.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'Zoe earned fifty-five dollars. That is her income. Her expenses were ten dollars. Profit is what is left after expenses, so fifty-five minus ten is forty-five. The profit is forty-five dollars.'
